https://www.dw.com/en/sudan-civil-war-wh.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Hedr Hundreds of thousands of Sudanese have been displaced Image: Sarah Vuylsteke/NRC/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement Flattened houses and rubble where a school once stood: These are the scenes that have appeared in footage of the Sudanese city of el-Obeid published by Ayin Network, a nonpartisan Sudanese media outlet. Drone attacks by the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have caused enormous damage to civilian infrastructure, including power grids, transformers, water treatment plants, schools, universities and hospitals in the capital of North Kordofan. The local population is struggling to survive, according to Ahmed Awad, a native of el-Obeid and a project manager for children's rights organization Plan International there. The city — whose population previously numbered half a million but has now become home to several hundred thousand people who are displaced — is under siege, he added. There is a shortage of medical supplies as well as food and safe, clean water, and Awad said he saw long lines of people at just one water pump: "Sometimes you can spend all day to get one liter of water for two or three days." Most of the time, children and teenagers are the ones sent to fetch water. Millions across Sudan are going hungry, including over 825,000 children under 5 suffering from severe acute malnutrition Image: AFP He added that a drone had hit a primary school and killed three children, which had caused trauma among other children, many of whom no longer dared go to school. "One of the mothers said three of her children cannot sleep because they are always in fear of something happening again," he said. Even when they're sitting in their classrooms, they live with the constant fear that a drone could strike at any moment. Awad and his colleagues at Plan International are working to provide psychological support to the affected children. Sudan's strategic crossroads El-Obeid is a strategically important location. The city is a trading hub in the middle of the desert on the only major route between Sudan's capital, Khartoum — which is controlled by the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) — and the western Darfur region, large parts of which are under the control of the RSF. El-Obeid is currently controlled by the army, which has some 13,000 soldiers stationed there, and has been on the front line since fighting shifted from Darfur to Kordofan at the beginning of the year. The RSF has deployed troops to about 30 kilometers (18.6 miles) beyond the city limits, and has been using drones to bomb civilian infrastructure. Warnings of mass atrocities Analysts, aid organizations and the United Nations have warned that the RSF could soon capture el-Obeid. They fear a similar scenario to that which unfolded in the city of el-Fasher in the neighboring state of North Darfur in October 2025, when the RSF began by bombing infrastructure before storming the city after an 18-month siege. Earlier this year, a UN Fact-Finding Mission for the Sudan presented to the United Nations Human Rights Council in Geneva detailed atrocities in the capture of el-Fasher and identified "hallmarks of genocide." “We warn that an escalation of the situation could lead to a repeat of the horrific human rights violations and abuses against civilians that we documented in Al-Fashir,” numerous human rights organizations said in a joint appeal. "We are alarmed by the ongoing hostilities around the city, including frequent drone strikes," said Pekka Haavisto, the UN chief's personal envoy for Sudan , in June. "These are already affecting the civilians and disrupting humanitarian aid to the city. Any further escalation of the situation would place thousands of people at risk." Growing up under drones The situation is particularly dire for the children trapped in el-Obeid, says Francesco Lanino, deputy country director of the children's charity Save the Children in Sudan. Drone attacks on schools and displacement camps have caused severe trauma. Lanino recently visited the Tawila displacement camp near el-Fashir in Darfur, which was taken over by the RSF in October. There, he encountered children struggling to process what had happened to them. "We met several children who refused to speak afterwards," Lanino said. Many found it difficult to understand why they had experienced such violence. Lanino is concerned about the long-term impact of the conflict. "If these traumas are not addressed, they could seek revenge, because all this stress, all this trauma, could erupt in a new wave of violence." Sudan's army has launched a new offensive in Kordofan from the capital, Khartoum, and says it has taken control of the 360-kilometer-long highway linking Omdurman, Khartoum's twin city, with el-Obeid. SAF Chief of Staff Abdel-Fattah al-Burhan recently inspected the newly captured areas in North Kordofan by helicopter and congratulated his troops. The advance has reopened supply routes to SAF units in El Obeid. Residents of the previously besieged city celebrated the arrival of army forces, as the immediate threat appears to have receded for now. As they retreated, RSF fighters looted markets and villages in North Kordofan and committed human rights violations against local residents, according to the Sudan Tribune media platform. Last Monday, RSF commander Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as "Hemeti," told commanders in the affected areas they no longer needed to wait for orders from the high command and could instead launch counteroffensives at their own discretion. The move could lead to further attacks on civilians and additional looting. Who are Sudan's RSF? https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: Police duties in Trinidad are being transferred to the Henderson county sheriff’s office until a permanent solution is found. Photograph: Trinidad Police Department via Facebook View image in fullscreen Police duties in Trinidad are being transferred to the Henderson county sheriff’s office until a permanent solution is found. Photograph: Trinidad Police Department via Facebook Texas Texas police department ordered closed for failing to provide any benefit to community Disbanding of department in Trinidad comes after arrest of a resident for posting about issues with local water supply Richard Luscombe Tue 15 Sep 2026 09.15 EDT Last modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 09.16 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A police department in Texas that arrested a local resident for complaining on social media about their city’s contaminated water supply has been ordered closed after failing to prove it provided any benefit to the community. State officials stepped in to investigate after Jennifer Combs spent a night in jail in May after a post appeared on her Facebook page suggesting people were hospitalized by bacteria in the water pipes of Trinidad, a municipality in Henderson county about 75 miles south-east of Dallas. The Trinidad police department’s then chief, Charles Gregory, said at the time that a since-dropped felony charge of making a false report or alarm for Combs was justified because the hospital claims were “simply false and have only caused unnecessary fear and confusion in our community”, Texas news station KDFW reported . The next day, Trinidad police arrested a supporter of Combs for misdemeanor disorderly conduct after he displayed a “fuck bad cops” placard outside city hall. That charge was also later dropped. The arrests prompted an investigation of Trinidad police by the Texas commission on law enforcement (TCLE). TCLE wrote to Trinidad’s mayor, Dennis Haws, on 9 September informing him that the agency would be disbanded. The letter, also reported by KDFW , said the department “failed to meet minimum standards” and “was unable to provide evidence that the agency provides public benefit to the community”. A separate investigation by the Texas commission on environmental quality found issues with Trinidad’s water supply that city officials have promised to fix. According to the news channel, the police department lacked resources for officers, including not having bulletproof vests or an evidence room. Other highlighted failings were problems with use-of-force policies, active shooter situations, vehicle pursuits and the professional conduct of officers. Haws told the outlet that the state’s order to revoke the city agency’s license to operate law enforcement was “not a shock”. He said: “There’s been a lot of neglect through the years. We are moving in a positive direction. We’ve got to get past all of this.” The department employed five full-time officers and several part-timers. Police duties in Trinidad are being transferred to the Henderson county sheriff’s office until a permanent solution is found. Gregory resigned in June after a grand jury declined to indict Combs. The citizen journalist has since filed a wrongful arrest lawsuit against Trinidad, claiming her detention was politically motivated retaliation for speaking out on the water issues. Henderson county judge Scott McKee, meanwhile, has said he was misled by the police department, which he said omitted key information when it asked him to approve an arrest warrant for Combs. After Trinidad police were ordered to disband, Combs posted a statement on social media saying: “For months, citizens who questioned this [agency] were dismissed, attacked and in my case arrested. Now the state agency responsible for regulating Texas law enforcement has confirmed that this department could not demonstrate compliance with even the minimum standards. “We were never the problem. We were exposing it.” The Guardian has contacted the city and police department for further comment. https://www.politico.eu/article/what-and.text: LONDON — When Keir Starmer had his first dinner with Donald Trump, he strained so hard to impress the U.S. president that his host offered the British team a second helping of chicken. Andy Burnham’s face-to-face introduction next Tuesday will look very different. Instead of the two-hour Trump Tower rendezvous that Starmer enjoyed in September 2024, British officials expect their new prime minister to sit down with his U.S. counterpart on relatively neutral ground in the United Nations headquarters at the far edge of Manhattan. Their meeting is currently penciled in for Tuesday afternoon, sandwiched between Burnham’s 15-minute address to the U.N. General Assembly on Tuesday evening and Trump’s morning speech to the same hall — which given his past form , may drown out other headlines with whatever he says there. Advertisement Advertisement That may prove convenient for Burnham. “There will be so much going on that it reduces the intensity and scrutiny,” said Claire Ainsley, a former aide to Starmer who is now at the center-left Progressive Policy Institute think tank. POLITICO spoke to a dozen current and former senior U.K. officials, ministers and MPs, many of them granted anonymity to speak frankly, about Burnham’s likely handling of the visit. Almost all predicted he would opt for a middle road somewhere between Starmer’s initial charm and the more combative approach of Canadian PM Mark Carney: Get in, smile, press the case for Ukraine, and try to leave without a major upset. Downing Street’s overwhelming priority for the New York visit has been to squeeze in an IRL meeting with Trump, with whom Burnham has now spoken to by phone twice, according to a person familiar with the preparations. It will allow the two men to engage but with far lower stakes than a one-to-one visit in Washington or London, just one of a series of leader meetings that blend into the noise of a multilateral summit. The hope, one U.K. government official said, is to “get the Trump meeting done and dusted in a relatively safe environment.” That was then The shift away from Starmer’s more high-pressure encounters is driven not so much by Burnham’s laid-back style — the new PM said last month he will “say what I feel” to Trump while also trying to “find a connection” — as by a profound change in the balance of risk since 2024. Advertisement Advertisement Burnham has less to prove. Starmer, who took office shortly before Trump’s second election victory, signed deals on tech, trade and pharmaceuticals from scratch. Warming to Trump was the “medicine required at that period,” said a U.K. diplomat. His successor’s job is to fix the mess of unresolved threads left behind. Burnham also has the benefit of hindsight, having watched Starmer’s efforts to praise Trump lead to embarrassment when the president lambasted the PM over the Iran conflict, oil drilling and tech taxes. Trump at one point even dissed Starmer as “no Winston Churchill.” Donald Trump shakes hands with Britain’s former prime minister Keir Starmer at a joint press conference at the White House on February 27, 2025. | Carl Court/Pool/AFP via Getty Images The new PM won’t “bend the knee in the way Starmer did,” predicted the same U.K. diplomat. He won’t be going to “kiss the ring,” added the first U.K. government official quoted above. “It’s completely different this time. There’s no drama about having to stay in his good books.” Yet Trump still has two years left in office, and a smooth relationship will be vital for the U.K. leader who has tried to keep his focus on domestic issues — but is watching his promises to ease living costs be buffeted by rising defense pressures and inflation from the Iran war. The two men will also meet at a point where Britain and its allies are turning their heads away from the U.S. Advertisement Advertisement Two years ago “Trump was at the height of his powers,” said one Starmer Cabinet minister. “The reality is different now.” While November’s looming midterm elections threaten to dent Trump’s authority at home, abroad his approaches to NATO and the Middle East have led European allies to find solace elsewhere. Britain and its allies are forming groups of so-called middle powers, while Carney pushes closer ties between Canada and the EU that will still be in negotiation long after Trump’s departure. And Burnham has repeatedly talked about strengthening ties with Brussels — seeing through a reset in relations that Starmer initiated. Olivia O’Sullivan, director of the U.K. in the World Programme at the Chatham House think tank, said the country is now “testing the waters” of loosening its strategic alignment with the U.S. — even as it continues to rely on America’s security and nuclear weapons architecture. (And even as Burnham continues to let the U.S. use Britain’s air bases for limited strikes on Iran.) Emily Thornberry, the Labour MP who chairs the House of Commons’ foreign affairs committee, said there’s a reason for that: “I think a couple of years ago, the hopes were high that Trump would help with Ukraine, we would have a proper trade deal, and so on. He hasn’t delivered on those things, so we’re getting used to the disappointment. We don’t expect as much.” One former senior official under Starmer put it more starkly: “The world is just viewing the United States differently. He is doing enormous long-term damage to the U.S.’s relationship with all of its allies. Institutions that have stood for decades can no longer do the jobs that they used to be able to do, because America is proving to be an unreliable ally. This is hugely significant in the long term.” No list of deliverables Burnham, whose two calls with Trump since July have both run far over their allotted time, is at least looking to keep things friendly. Advertisement Advertisement The new prime minister is not expected to take a big list of deliverables or policy goals into his meeting, two people familiar with the planning said. Burnham is expected to press Trump on U.S. support for Ukraine after paying his first overseas trip there last month. British officials hope there is now a more pro-Ukraine atmosphere on Capitol Hill after the House of Representatives passed a sweeping Russia sanctions bill long championed by the late Senator Lindsay Graham. Thornberry said the PM should urge Trump to speed up supplies of Patriot missiles to Ukraine ahead of the winter. Ukraine’s forces are “winning without the Americans, but they could actually win if the Americans did help,” she added. Andy Burnham visits the scene of Russian strikes on Lukanivska Market in Kyiv, Ukraine on August 24, 2026. | Henry Nicholls/WPA Pool/Getty Images Britain’s wider activities at UNGA — which Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband will also attend — could be dominated by a clash over the hardening stance of the U.K., France and Canada against Israel. The three countries issued joint sanctions against West Bank settlements earlier in September, after what one U.K. official described as a “tag team” coordination effort between Miliband, Burnham and the leaders and foreign ministers of allied countries. The U.K. is hoping to use UNGA to work on the next steps in the humanitarian response for Gaza. British officials are privately hopeful that the U.S. response will continue to be muted; two U.K. government officials said they believed Secretary of State Marco Rubio viewed the intervention as helpful, given it applies pressure to Israel without it coming from the U.S. Burnham faces a choice about how hard to lean into the issue of the Middle East in his own speech to UNGA. His closest No. 10 aides have kept a “tight hold” on the thinking around his remarks, said the person with knowledge of the planning quoted above. Advertisement Advertisement Whatever he chooses, plenty of dangers lie in wait — not least Trump’s views on oil and gas in the North Sea. Industry figures believe Burnham’s government has delayed a decision on whether to drill at two fields until after an Oct. 8 special election to replace Starmer, where Labour is battling the Green Party. Trump has long been perplexed by the delay. Burnham’s government has also delayed a key decision on defense spending until 2027, despite pressure from the U.S. to set out a clearer timetable. And Britain is stuck over how to proceed with its deal giving up sovereignty of the Chagos Islands, a strategically crucial archipelago in the Indian Ocean, after Trump disowned the pact earlier this year. Mauritius — the beneficiary — could agitate at UNGA to unfreeze the deal. But it’s the issue of artificial intelligence that has lately rocketed up the news agenda. Here, Burnham faces a conundrum. On the one hand, Britain can sell a “third way” in AI development between Trump’s free-for-all and burdensome regulation in the EU, argued Emily Darlington, a Labour MP and member of the Commons Science and Technology Committee. “There are things that [U.S. tech firms] need from us, not least some of the really advanced stuff that we’re doing around quantum, and in the future neuromorphic computing,” she said. “We’re a huge market for them. Large language models are desperate to train on British material that goes back centuries. The BBC archive, all of these sorts of things, are what they’re desperate for. There’s a bit of a fight over whether there is a British advantage to allowing them access to that material, and so there is a bit of a negotiation.” Advertisement Yet the U.K.’s digital services tax has drawn Trump’s repeated ire, while PoliticsHome reported this week that U.S. officials warned Britain at the London embassy against its online safety restrictions and plans to ban under-16s from social media. One minister said Burnham’s conversation “can’t be on the digital services tax or regulation like the Online Safety Act, because there’s a tangible risk Trump will go ballistic.” ‘Andy has been a lucky general’ The same minister suggested Burnham will want the sort of relationship that Tony Blair had with George Bush — respectful, even if not as equals. It is a tall order for a president as mercurial as Trump, yet old allies of Starmer insist he paved the way for it. They point to Starmer’s decision to push back against Trump to defend Greenland’s sovereignty, to bring together a “coalition of the willing” for Ukraine and to welcome Kyiv’s leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy after Trump hectored him in the Oval Office. Volodymyr Zelensky shakes hands with Andy Burnham ahead of their bilateral meeting at Horodetskyi House in Kyiv, Ukraine, on August 24, 2026. | Henry Nicholls/WPA Pool/Getty Images Starmer was not being nice to Trump because he liked him, argued the Starmer Cabinet minister quoted earlier in this story, but because he had to bring him back from the brink on NATO and Ukraine. It means Burnham has inherited an established relationship in which he has no need to lavish the president with praise. All he has to do, argue some, is avoid a barrage of abuse on Truth Social. “Andy has been a lucky general in the calming of Trump,” argued one U.K. official who worked under Starmer. “Keir was dealing with a completely different beast.” And yet, this person added: “It could all change in the space of two weeks.” Esther Webber contributed reporting. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cked.text: Figure caption, On the ground in Pakistan as school roof collapse kills more than 30 children By Bilal Ahmed and Azizullah Khan ,Â BBC Urdu ,Â Reporting from Peshawar Â and Â Phelan Chatterjee Published 15 October 2026, 07:49 BST Updated 45 minutes ago At least 33 pupils and a teacher have been killed after a school roof collapsed in the north-western Pakistani city of Peshawar, according to hospital officials. More than a dozen others are injured, with some in a critical condition. Emergency services were called to the private Al-Khair school in Dir Colony at 08:48 (03:48 GMT) on Thursday after lessons had begun, rescue official Bilal Faizi told the BBC. The roof of an upper-floor classroom had collapsed, he said, causing ceilings below to cave in and trap children beneath the debris. Announcing the arrest of the school's owner, police chief Mian Saeed promised a thorough inquiry into "whether there were any violations of building codes". Warning: This article contains distressing details An English teacher from a nearby school said he immediately rushed to the site with other local residents when they heard sirens and the sound of ambulances. Together, they pulled more than 20 children from the rubble, he said. "I personally pulled out six children with my own hands. Most of them were alive and talking. But later it was found that they had passed away." "There was a lot of blood," he said. "One child said he was in a lot of pain. His tongue had dried up in his mouth, [and he was] asking for water." Sohail, another local resident, said he and others tried to remove children from under the rubble "using shovels". Image source, Reuters Image caption, A rescue worker said an upper-floor roof collapsed, crashing through three classrooms The school building had been constructed on a temporary basis, according to emergency official Arif Khattak. Earlier reports suggested the destroyed classrooms were in a two-storey part of the building, but Peshawar police chief Mian Saeed later confirmed that classrooms on three floors had been brought down. There were about 30 pupils in the top class, 40 in the middle and 45 on the ground floor, he said. It appears that when the roof of the top-floor classroom collapsed, the falling rubble crashed through classrooms below, bringing their ceilings down too. Saeed said the entire structure, which had "substandard" roof slabs, was "overloaded" and beyond the limit of how much weight it could bear. The school is on a very narrow street, meaning it was difficult for rescue workers to reach the site and transport the injured to hospitals. Peshawar's Lady Reading Hospital reported the deaths of 32 children and a teacher while Naseerullah Khan Babar Memorial Hospital reported one child dead. The police chief said the building was still "extremely dangerous" and urged people to move away. The Governor of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Faisal Karim Kundi, has ordered a safety audit of all schools in the province to "identify potential risks and ensure that immediate corrective measures are taken wherever necessary". "We cannot allow the safety of our children to be compromised," he said. Furious family members of deceased pupils accused the school of ignoring safety concerns. "Make an example of them, a lesson for all," Mohammad Zaman, a man who lost two nephews in the disaster, told Reuters news agency. Image source, Reuters Image caption, The roof crashed through three classrooms and buried schoolchildren in debris, police say Image source, Reuters In June, fourteen children died after the roof of a private tuition centre near Lahore collapsed. And in August, 14 newborn babies were killed by a fire that ripped through a neonatal unit at a hospital in the capital, Islamabad, which an inquiry found lacked fire alarms and sprinklers . https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqkg.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Thousands gathered at Krakow's historic Market Square to honour the victims of Saturday's attack By Sarah Rainsford Southern and Eastern Europe correspondent ,Â Reporting from Krakow Published 9 hours ago Thousands of people joined a silent march through central Krakow on Monday night, in memory of those killed and injured when a gunman went on a violent rampage at the weekend. The crowd were led by Poland's president and prime minister, the bitter political rivals putting on a rare show of unity after the country's deadliest attack in modern times. As they reached the historic Market Square, a bugler played from the tower. Many people were carrying flowers or candles to leave at the shrines that now dot the cobblestones, each one marking a spot where someone died. Fiercely proud of its reputation for safety, Poland has been profoundly shaken by this attack. It has left people struggling to make some kind of sense of what happened. The alleged gunman has been named as 24-year-old Michal Oksinski by local media. Critically injured in a shoot-out with police, he did not regain consciousness and died in hospital early on Monday . Initially, the interior minister claimed that Oksinski was driven by far-right, extremist views. The national prosecutor's office now says that it is too soon to say he was "inspired" by any ideology. "The minister wanted to win domestic political points. That's not responsible behaviour," Pawel Musialek of the Jagiellonian University suggests, in a country where politics is highly - and often viciously - polarised. "So far we've seen no clear message that this guy was strongly ideological, and that it's not more like something from the darknet." There has been no mention of any letter or manifesto that Oksinski left. One neighbour told Polish news site Onet that the 24-year-old was a "bit of a loner" but few who knew him well have spoken publicly. What we know so far after Krakow gun attack Published 22 hours ago In addition to his electronic devices like his phone, investigators are examining a number of badges that Oksinski had attached to his military-style outfit. The prosecutor's office says a yellow Gadsden flag with a coiled snake symbol was displayed in his bedroom. "It has various meanings of freedom and rebellion," a spokesman emphasised. "Not necessarily negative." It was at Oksinski's home that the bodies of his parents and sister were discovered. It is alleged that he shot them, before driving some 200km (125 miles) south to continue the killing in Krakow. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Candles and flowers have been placed around the square in places where someone died Two days on, shops and cafes around the market square are beginning to fill up again, but the mood is subdued. A Zara clothes shop is still boarded up, after bullets smashed the glass. A local man in his 50s died just outside. Jo, a Scottish tourist, saw paramedics "who got there ridiculously fast", fighting to save him. "It was all pretty grim." Like many, she initially mistook the rifle shots for fireworks. On the opposite corner of the square, beside another cluster of flowers, people keep pausing to take pictures of the holes that were blasted into the wall by gunfire. One of the six victims has been identified as a Polish painter in her 50s, who was a mother of four, and in town with friends for an exhibition opening. A British citizen and an Austrian who died are yet to be named publicly. Several drivers of the horse-drawn carriages that are usually poised to trot tourists around the square were seriously injured. Image caption, Olha, a Ukrainian citizen, moved to Krakow for safety when Russia launched its full-scale invasion Olha, who works in a nearby chocolate shop says everyone is now nervous. On Saturday, people rushed into her store to escape the gunman who was tearing around in his car, firing through the window. Olha is Ukrainian, and moved to Krakow when Russia invaded. "We left our own country for safety. This is supposed to be a safe place!" she said. "It's so sad, and so scary. Especially that he drove all the way here for two hours, planning this and thinking about it." She regrets that the gunman did not survive: "So many are dead, so many lives have been ruined, and now there will be no justice." Image source, Filip Radwanski/Anadolu via Getty Images Image caption, Political differences were set aside between President Karol Nawrocki (left) and Prime Minister Donald Tusk (right) at the vigil on Monday When Oksinski's car was searched, four firearms and "hundreds of rounds of ammunition" were found, all owned legally by the alleged killer and his father. Both were members of the Swit Starachowice sports club, where there is a shooting range. A spokesman recalls Michal Oksinski as unremarkable: average competition results and normal behaviour. He had been just three times this year, most recently in August with his father. The club spokesman is adamant that it does not train combat firing, only shooting from a fixed point. Gun ownership in Poland has grown considerably since war broke out in Ukraine just across the border, but this is the first mass shooting anyone here can remember. Inevitably, it has brought scrutiny of the checks over who qualifies to handle such weapons, including psychological tests, as Michal Oksinski passed all of them. On Monday, the government announced an urgent review. Image caption, "Thank you Mr Policemen, get better soon" At the spot where Oksinski's car was intercepted and he was shot by police there is another memorial, this one in honour of the officers still in hospital. Some have brought flowers, but a girl called Bianka has left a card that reads: "Thank you Mr Policemen, get better soon." A couple of steps away, there's a series of bullet holes in the glass. "This man was a real hero, he didn't hesitate," Ania says, referring to officer Jakub Kulik who was shot in the chest. His condition remains serious. "We're here to help him fight for his life." "Nothing like this has never happened before, it's terrible," a young man called Wojtek tells me. He's only glad that the gunman responsible for such horror turned out to be Polish. "People here are already against immigration, so that would have been even worse." Ania thinks Poles will pull through, though the country's image as a low-crime oasis has been shattered. Most of all, she's angry that Michal Oksinski died without being held to account for the devastation. "I think we deserve to know why."
